question: At 25 training positions the state policy solved 18 of 30 held-out rollouts and vision solved none. Is that a shortage of data? Does the score climb with 50, 100, 200 and 400 positions?
measure: Successes out of 30 on the same 10 held-out positions (3 repeats each) at every data size, plus safety frames. The test set is frozen: the same for every row and never tuned on.
outcome: Yes. The state policy reached 30/30 with zero safety frames at 400 positions. Vision at a fixed 20,000 steps was erratic (0, 6, 14, 9, 18), but at 400 positions and 120,000 steps three seeds scored 24, 30 and 24 out of 30.
setup: A policy is the network that drives the arm. The teacher is a hand-written script that does the task using the cube's exact position from the simulator; the policy is trained to copy the teacher's recorded commands. The policy outputs a chunk: the next 90 commands at once. A seed is the random number that starts training; the same recipe with a different seed gives a different policy. A rollout is one full attempt. A safety frame is one step where the policy asks a joint to leave its allowed range or to move faster than the per-step cap; a rollout with safety frames does not count. The state policy reads the cube's exact position from the simulator. The vision policy gets the wrist camera image, the joint commands and a progress clock: inputs a real arm has. Held-out positions are test positions never used in training. The gripper clamp clips the gripper command to its limits at run time; from this experiment on the vision policy carries it too. The previous experiment built a generator of random cube positions that keeps only positions the teacher completes cleanly, trained on 25 of them, and got 18/30 (state) and 0/30 (vision) on 10 held-out positions. The state failures sat where the 25 positions left gaps. Here the same recipe is repeated on bigger training sets, one new set per size. An epoch is one pass over the training data: at a fixed number of steps, more data means fewer passes over each example.

parts.title: Does the held-out score climb with more training positions?
parts.why: If the failures are coverage gaps, more positions should fill them with no change to the recipe.
parts.did: For each size: generate a screened set of positions, record the teacher with frames, train the state policy (width 512, 90,000 steps) and the vision policy (20,000 steps), and test both on the frozen 10 positions.
parts.conclusion: For the state policy, data coverage was the whole story: 18, then 27 at three sizes (a different single position failing each time), then 30/30 with zero safety frames at 400. That is the first perfect held-out score in the project. Vision at fixed steps goes up and down, which more data alone does not explain.

parts.title: Is vision short of data or short of training?
parts.why: With steps fixed at 20,000, each example is seen less often as the data grows. Data size and training per example change together, so the vision column mixes two effects.
parts.did: A probe: the same 200-position data, trained for 60,000 steps instead of 20,000.
parts.conclusion: Three times the steps on the same data turned 9/30 into 24/30. Vision was starved of training, not of data. The rule from here on: training steps scale with the size of the dataset.

parts.title: Vision at 400 positions with training scaled to match
parts.why: If vision with enough training approaches the state policy's 30/30, then a policy using only inputs a real arm has can do the task on unseen positions.
parts.did: Trained vision on the 400-position recording for 120,000 steps (about the same number of passes, roughly 40 epochs, as the 60,000-step probe on 200 positions) on seeds 101, 202 and 303.
parts.conclusion: Mean 26/30. Seed 202 is the first perfect held-out score from camera input alone. The spread across seeds (24 to 30) says the recipe is not yet robust to the seed. Under-trained vision is also unsafe vision: 642 safety frames at 20,000 steps against 0, 0 and 3 at 120,000.

trust.text: The same frozen 10 held-out positions (30 rollouts) for every row, never tuned on.
The state recipe is unchanged across all sizes; only the amount of teacher data changes.
The probe changes only the number of steps on the same 200-position data.
The success counts and safety frames in the tables match the sweep logs (SWEEP_LOG.txt and VISION_N400_LOG.txt).
One state policy and one vision policy per data size, so the 27, 27, 27 plateau and the vision zigzag each rest on single runs.
The 25-position vision row has no gripper clamp; the other vision rows do.
10 test positions: one failing position moves the score by 3 of 30. All positions are ones the teacher can solve.
Exploratory mode: nothing registered before the run. The note says a promotion claim on either 30/30 needs a pre-registered gate first.
The research log notes that all of August ran on a simulator whose joint map and camera later turned out to be wrong, so these numbers do not transfer to the real arm.

meaning: Both gaps from the previous experiment were about scale. The state policy needed more positions and nothing else. The vision policy needed more positions and training that grows with them. The core question of the vision rung, whether pixels can replace the privileged cube position, is answered yes in this simulator at 400 positions. It is a promising recipe and not a finished one: two of three seeds stop at 24/30. The note's options from here are more data or more training per seed for robustness, and a pre-registered gate if either 30/30 is to be claimed formally. The sweep also forced two pieces of infrastructure: streaming writes for frame files larger than RAM (38 GB at 400 positions), and frame prefetching that made vision training 3.2 times faster with bitwise-identical results.
lesson: Scale training steps with the data. A curve drawn at fixed steps can make more data look useless when the model is only under-trained.

log:
**TL;DR:** More random positions alone took the state policy to a perfect 30/30,
and vision reached 24-30/30 once training time grew with the data.

**Problem.** At 25 positions, the state policy got 18/30 and vision 0/30.

*How we know:* the state policy failed exactly where the 25 positions left gaps
(entry 16). I didn't know if vision would follow.

**Experiment.** Same recipe, same 10 test positions, training on 50, 100, 200
and 400 positions. Vision first at a fixed 20k steps, then at 400 positions with
120k steps on 3 seeds.

*What we hope to learn:* if it's a data problem, the curve climbs.

**Outcome.**

| positions | state | vision (20k steps) |
|---|---|---|
| 50 | 27/30 | 6/30 |
| 100 | 27/30 | 14/30 |
| 200 | 27/30 | 9/30 |
| 400 | **30/30**, 0 bad frames | 18/30, 642 bad frames |

Vision at 400 positions and 120k steps: 24, 30 and 24 out of 30 across seeds.

- Fixed steps with more data means fewer passes over each example, and vision
  needs more of them. Like doubling the reading list without more study time.
- Undertrained vision is unsafe vision: 642 bad frames at 400 positions and 20k
  steps.

*Note:* all of August ran on a sim whose joint map and camera turned out to be
wrong (entries 20-21), so these numbers don't transfer to the real arm. The
lessons do.

**Takeaway:** scale training steps with the data. And one 30/30 seed with
others at 24 is a promising recipe, not a solved one.
